extracted.intended_audience: Regulatory analysts, rule writers, and agency decisionmakers at U.S. federal executive agencies (heads of executive agencies and establishments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses and regulatory accounting statements to support proposed and final federal rules, specifying required elements, analytic approaches (BCA/CEA), alternative consideration, specialized legal requirements, and reporting conventions under Executive Order 12866 and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Elements of a Regulatory Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With these elements you should be able to assess quantitatively the benefits and costs of the proposed rule and its alternatives. A complete analysis includes discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs and a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain causal linkage from rule actions to expected benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (e.g., indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a similar analysis for each alternative. Linkages should be explicit so readers can judge plausibility of benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a baseline for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline against which benefits and costs are defined; normally the 'no action' baseline but comparisons to a 'next best' alternative may be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what the world will be like absent the proposed rule; use the baseline consistently when estimating incremental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify side-effects and ancillary benefits/costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives; add these to direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both direct and ancillary effects in the accounting and discuss their likely importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete regulatory analysis includes a discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs, and identifies important non-monetary values at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If non-quantified effects may be important, carry out threshold (break-even) analysis and indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out the opinions of those who will be affected by the regulation and those with special knowledge or insight; early consultation is encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation helps ensure analyses address relevant issues and that pertinent data are available; do not limit consultation to final stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use competent professional judgment (no formulaic approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality regulatory analysis requires competent professional judgment; different regulations may call for different emphases depending on complexity and sensitivity to assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no mechanical formula—explain choices, assumptions, and why certain factors were emphasized or deprioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of assumptions, methods, and data
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: state assumptions (time horizon, discount rates), provide sensitivity analysis, cite sources, include appendices documenting models and methods, and include an executive summary and standardized accounting statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency should enable a qualified third party to see how estimates and conclusions were derived; provide full documentation and references and make sensitivity/uncertainty analyses available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of need for Federal regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, agencies must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary, describe statutory authority, extent of discretion, and regulatory instruments considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether action addresses a significant market failure or other compelling public need and show that government intervention is likely to do more good than harm; present strengths and limitations for intangible rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of market failures and other social purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain whether the action addresses market failures (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) or other social purposes (improving government functioning, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy, personal freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe market failures qualitatively and where feasible quantitatively; document information-processing problems if invoked; justify non-market-failure rationales carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Externalities, common property resources, and public goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize externalities, common property resource problems (congestion/overuse), and public goods as types of market failure that can justify regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain nature of the externality, transactions costs or ill-defined property rights, and why private bargaining would not resolve the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market power considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether firms exercise market power that warrants regulation and beware that government action can itself create market power; consider whether validating a monopoly is justified (natural monopoly cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider technological change that may alter economies of scale and competition; avoid regulations that unnecessarily increase market power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate or asymmetric information
rubrics_metrics.description: If inadequate or asymmetric information is alleged, the analysis must document the nature of the problem and whether market-supplied information is inadequate to protect consumers or users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that information-processing errors or costly evaluation justify intervention; mere possibility of poor processing is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that federal action is the appropriate jurisdictional level
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternatives to federal regulation including antitrust, litigation, administrative compensation, state/local regulation, and international harmonization; justify federal role especially when spillovers or interstate effects exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether state/local experimentation or varying preferences argue against federal preemption; assess costs of regulatory fragmentation and trade effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain types of economic regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A demanding burden of proof is required to justify: (a) price controls in competitive markets; (b) production or sales quotas in competitive markets; (c) mandatory uniform quality standards where voluntary or disclosure could suffice; (d) controls on entry into employment or production (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulations that impose these constraints unless clearly necessary (e.g., health/safety entry controls or managing common property resources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative regulatory approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Once federal action is appropriate, agencies should consider a range of alternative regulatory approaches and eliminate some by preliminary analysis, retaining a manageable set for detailed evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance thorough exploration with practical limits on analytical capacity; modify regulation attributes or provisions to identify reasonable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different choices defined by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When statute prescribes specific requirements but allows discretion, examine benefits and costs of reasonable alternatives reflecting statutory discretion, including the statutory requirement itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare more and less stringent interpretations consistent with the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how alternative compliance dates affect net benefits and costs; timing can substantially change outcomes (e.g., lead times for industry or losses from delayed protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider staging, lead times, and transitional arrangements to minimize costs or losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different enforcement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate alternative enforcement and compliance frameworks (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, noncompliance penalties, random monitoring, parametric monitoring) and identify the most cost-effective enforcement scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differences in monitoring costs and effectiveness; choose enforcement that provides appropriate incentives at least cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of regulatory stringency to understand relationship between stringency and size/distribution of benefits and costs; benefits and costs generally rise with stringency but marginal benefits may decline while marginal costs rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate incremental benefits and costs for successive levels of stringency to identify efficient tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements by firm size
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider different requirements for large and small firms based on differences in compliance costs or expected benefits, recognizing small firms may face larger fixed compliance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure requirements do not inefficiently penalize small or productive firms; remember Regulatory Flexibility Act triggers for significant impacts on many small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements by geographic region
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefits or costs vary significantly by region, consider regionally-differentiated requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh regional tailoring against costs of regulatory fragmentation and potential inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance standards rather than design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer performance standards (outcomes-based) over design/engineering standards because they allow flexibility to achieve objectives cost-effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for monitoring or compliance assurance costs required to enforce performance standards and weigh those against cost savings from flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-oriented approaches rather than direct controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore economic-incentive alternatives (fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits/offsets, changes in liability/property rights, bonds/insurance) which can reduce costs or accelerate benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ABT (averaging, banking, trading) and other market mechanisms but evaluate local effects like 'hot spots' and distributional outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational measures rather than regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If market failure is due to information problems, prefer informational remedies (testing/rating systems, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) where effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate benefits and costs of informational measures, including displaced information, misinterpretation, and incentives to overinvest in disclosed attributes; consider least intrusive effective informational alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use both Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) as appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Both BCA and CEA provide frameworks for evaluating outcomes. Major rulemakings should be supported by both where possible: prepare a CEA for major health/safety rulemakings when a valid effectiveness measure exists; perform a BCA for major health/safety rulemakings when valid monetary values can be assigned; for other major rulemakings, carry out a BCA and add a CEA if primary benefits cannot be monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no quantified information can be produced, present a qualitative discussion of the issues and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCA: express benefits and costs in monetary units and use incremental analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In BCA both benefits and costs are expressed in monetary units so different policy attributes can be compared using a common measure; measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives to identify alternatives that maximize net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use benefit-cost ratios alone to rank alternatives; the size of net benefits (benefits minus costs) is the meaningful indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: When benefits/costs cannot be monetized, measure physically or describe qualitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: If a benefit or cost cannot be expressed in monetary units, try to measure it in physical units; if that is not possible, describe it qualitatively and rank its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct threshold analysis where appropriate to show how large non-quantified values would need to be to alter conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEA: careful construction of cost and effectiveness measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct CEA measures carefully: include all relevant societal costs (public and private), avoid double-counting, and choose effectiveness measures that capture final outcomes (lives saved, life-years) rather than intermediate outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incremental CEA when comparing alternatives; be cautious with average ratios and ensure effectiveness measures reflect variability in quality (e.g., acres of wetlands differ in ecological benefit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting and inappropriate adjustments in CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure net-cost numerator excludes benefits already used in the effectiveness denominator (e.g., don't reduce gross costs by a monetary valuation of life if life-years are used as the effectiveness measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some ancillary benefits are monetized but primary effectiveness is not, subtract monetized ancillary benefits from gross costs to yield a net cost estimate and acknowledge potential overstatement of cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer final outcome measures and consider integrated measures (QALYs, ELs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For public health and safety rulemakings, prefer final outcomes (lives saved, life-years) and consider integrated measures such as equivalent lives (ELs) or quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) to account for morbidity as well as mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of restrictive assumptions behind integrated measures (e.g., QALY assumptions about tradeoffs across remaining lifespan) and consider willingness-to-pay measures when appropriate; ensure fairness adjustments as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty: make assumptions explicit and use sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimates depend heavily on assumptions, make those assumptions explicit and carry out sensitivity analyses using plausible alternative assumptions; provide expected-value estimates and distributions where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If net-benefit signs or rankings change under plausible alternatives, conduct further analysis; provide 5th and 95th percentile bounds when possible and be transparent about uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume risk neutrality unless justified otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: In general assume 'risk neutrality' in benefit-cost calculations; if a different risk preference is adopted, explain the reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about any deviation from risk neutrality and present sensitivity to risk preference assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Regulatory Flexibility Act (small entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, prepare a proposed and final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (RFA) if the rule could have 'a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities'; consult SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy and consider posting RFAs online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow agency guidelines on RFA preparation; Executive Order 13272 requires notifying the Advocacy Office of draft rules with significant impacts on small entities; SBREFA consultations apply for EPA and OSHA and are encouraged for other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Unfunded Mandates Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Unfunded Mandates Act, prepare a written statement about benefits and costs prior to issuing a proposed or final rule that may result in aggregate expenditures by state/local/tribal governments or the private sector of $100,000,000 or more in any one year (adjusted for inflation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical requirements under EO 12866 are similar; the same analysis can often satisfy both requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Paperwork Reduction Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the rule will create additional information collection, paperwork, or recordkeeping burdens; OMB approval is required for new collections imposed on 10 or more persons and a valid OMB control number must be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure information collections are justified by practical utility; consult agency CIO for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Information Quality Guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis used to support rulemaking must meet agency and OMB information quality standards (per the Information Quality Law and OMB government-wide guidelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow agency information quality guidelines and consult OMB/staff (e.g., Statistical and Science Policy Branch) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider environmental impacts pursuant to NEPA and related statutes; prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) for major federal actions significantly affecting the human environment and complete NEPA documentation before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CEQ regulations (40 C.F.R. 1500-1508) and associated CEQ guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Impacts on children (EO 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Executive Order 13045, for economically significant rules that concern environmental health or safety risks likely to disproportionately affect children, provide OMB/OIRA an evaluation of the effects on children and an explanation of why the planned regulation is preferable to other feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address disproportionate risks to children to the extent permitted by law and consistent with agency mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized analytic requirements — Energy impacts (EO 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Executive Order 13211, prepare and submit to OMB a Statement of Energy Effects for significant energy actions, detailing adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use for the action and reasonable alternatives; publish the statement or a summary in the NPRM and final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB Memorandum guidance (e.g., Memorandum 01-27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and tabular reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule; report estimates using the guidance provided and a suggested format (form linked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting statements should present monetized and non-monetized effects clearly and include footnotes and documentation as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories for reporting benefits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Report benefit and cost estimates within mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories: (1) monetized and quantified, (2) quantified but not monetized, and (3) qualitative (not quantified or monetized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting across categories and use as many categories as necessary to describe major redistributive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying and monetizing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop quantitative estimates and convert them to dollar amounts if possible; many quantified estimates are readily convertible to dollar equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conversion to dollars is feasible, do so; otherwise present physical measures and qualitative descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize and rank qualitative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize or rank qualitative effects in terms of importance (certainty, likely magnitude, reversibility) and distinguish effects likely to be significant from those likely to be minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explanation of relative importance to help decisionmakers weigh qualitative factors against monetized estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time and discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic time horizon and annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%; report monetized effects in 2001 dollars and convert other-year dollars using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the stream in the year the final rule begins to have effects; annualized streams should reflect the appropriate horizon even if rule takes effect later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting on precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect feasible precision. For example, $220 million implies rounding to nearest $10 million (precision +/- $5 million); $222 million implies rounding to nearest $1 million (precision +/- $0.5 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rounding that communicates the precision of the estimate without implying false accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide distributions, expected values, and confidence bounds for uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions about estimates where such information exists; when only upper and lower bounds are provided, use 95th and 5th percentile bounds where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles of full disclosure apply; when uncertainty critically affects conclusions, describe benefits and costs under plausible alternative assumptions and add documentation or warnings as footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers versus welfare effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs; distinguish transfers from efficiency effects and between government and non-government transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sufficient categories to describe major redistributive effects and report efficiency effects of transfers separately if significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify distributional impacts (state/local/tribal/small_business/wages/growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by state, local, and tribal governments and, to the extent feasible, effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs under $1 billion are likely to have minimal effects on economic growth; provide disaggregated impacts where feasible.
